Data companion · Patent institutions

Irish patents and patent institutions

Ireland retained a separate patent system until 1852. These figures examine who used it, what they patented, and how patenting rates in Ireland and Great Britain compared before and after the introduction of UK-wide patent protection.

01 / Institutions

A separate system until 1852

England, Scotland and Ireland maintained separate patent systems. Protection obtained in one jurisdiction did not automatically extend to the others, so inventors seeking wider coverage had to obtain additional patents. Ireland’s register consequently records demand for protection in Ireland, including from patentees domiciled elsewhere (Billington, 2021).

The Patent Law Amendment Act of 1852 established a central Patent Office in London and replaced separate grants with UK-wide protection. Initial fees fell to £25, but maintaining protection for the full fourteen-year term required renewal payments of £50 after three years and £100 after seven. The reform reduced the upfront cost, although renewal decisions depended on patentees’ financial resources as well as the expected returns to their inventions (MacLeod et al., 2003).

The 1883 Act, effective from 1884, cut initial fees from £25 to £4. Renewal remained costly, but the first £50 payment was postponed until the end of the fourth year and annual instalments became an option. Applications rose from around 6,000 in 1883 to over 17,000 in 1884, reflecting a greater propensity to patent without evidence of a corresponding increase in innovation. Limited examination was introduced, but no prior-art search: registration still did not certify novelty (Nicholas, 2011).

02 / Comparison

Irish patenting in British perspective

The datasets used here distinguish patenting by Irish residents from patenting in Ireland. The comparative series measures Irish and British patentees relative to population, using English patents before 1852 and UK patents thereafter. The Irish register instead records use of Ireland’s separate system, including by patentees domiciled elsewhere. Changes across 1852 therefore reflect both institutional reform and wider coverage.

Patenting, skills and market opportunities

Billington (2021) examines English patents granted between 1700 and 1841 and their extension to Scotland and Ireland. Skilled patentees used the system more intensively and patented inventions with higher estimated economic value. Extension into other jurisdictions was more closely associated with an invention’s value than with its inventor’s occupational background, suggesting that expected returns helped determine where protection was sought.

These findings caution against treating the gap in patenting rates as a direct measure of inventive capacity. Patenting reflected skills and expected returns, and may also have depended on access to finance.

03 / Patentees in Ireland

Who patented in Ireland?

The Irish patent system was used overwhelmingly by patentees domiciled outside Ireland. Between 1800 and 1852, it contains 1,670 patent–patentee entries, of which 77 record an Irish domicile, 1,542 a domicile in Great Britain, and 51 elsewhere.

The predominance of patentees domiciled in Great Britain is consistent with the idea that Irish and Scottish patents functioned as top-up certificates to extend English patents to additional UK markets. The register therefore captures demand for patent rights in Ireland as well as invention by Irish residents. The topic comparison in the next section distinguishes these groups within the Irish system; it does not compare Irish inventions with the full population of British patents.

What is being counted?

The complete register covers 1708–1852 and contains 1,718 patent–patentee entries. The annual chart shows the 1,670 entries dated 1800–1852. A patent with two patentees contributes two entries, and a person appears again for each patent.

The topic comparison below instead groups entries using the supplied patent number. This produces 1,496 numbered records plus one unnumbered patent, giving 1,497 records. It is a count of register records, not a reconstruction of invention families.

04 / Patent topics

Different patterns of invention

Compare the topic shares for the complete register and the period after the Union.

Why these categories, and how were patents classified?

We use the twenty classes defined by Billington and Hanna (2021, Table 7). Their taxonomy draws on 35 existing classification schemes, review by an experienced patent examiner, and topic analysis across patent datasets. Designed around inventions’ principal economic application, it provides a published basis for comparison and was applied by its authors to British patents from 1700 to 1850.

We applied their definitions to the Irish register descriptions using AI-assisted coding and review. Each patent receives one primary class; all twenty classes are retained. This applies their taxonomy rather than replicating their topic-modelling procedure. The assignments remain provisional, and the catalogue records the reasoning behind them.

Domicile, joint patentees and data checks

Recorded domicile need not identify a patentee’s origins. A London address may obscure an Irish connection, but the register contains no birthplace field with which to assess this. The figures therefore measure recorded domicile, not ancestry.

Seventy patents involve only Irish-domiciled patentees and three involve both Irish and other domiciles. These form the Irish group of 73. A further 1,422 involve only recorded domiciles elsewhere. Two have no recorded domicile and are omitted from the comparison. No patent is counted in both comparison groups.

The unnumbered record for James Blyth Waynman (1826, “Hat bodies”) is retained separately. Record 13030 has two years, 1849 and 1850, attached to the same description under different patentees. Both years are retained; the patent is counted once in the pooled topic comparison. One patent changes the Irish group’s share by approximately 1.37 percentage points.

06 / Sources and methods

Sources & downloads

The figures use data provided by Stephen Billington, presented and analysed by Christopher L. Colvin and Eoin McLaughlin. Their coverage and units differ; the Irish-register totals should not be added to the comparative series.

  1. MacLeod, Christine, Jennifer Tann, James Andrew, and Jeremy Stein (2003). “Evaluating Inventive Activity: The Cost of Nineteenth-Century UK Patents and the Fallibility of Renewal Data.” The Economic History Review, 56(3), 537–562. doi:10.1111/j.1468-0289.2003.00261.x.
  2. Nicholas, Tom (2011). “Cheaper patents.” Research Policy, 40(2), 325–339. doi:10.1016/j.respol.2010.10.012.
  3. Billington, Stephen D. (2021). “What explains patenting behaviour during Britain’s Industrial Revolution?” Explorations in Economic History, 82, 101426. doi:10.1016/j.eeh.2021.101426.
  4. Billington, Stephen D., and Alan J. Hanna (2021). “That’s Classified! Inventing a New Patent Taxonomy.” Industrial and Corporate Change, 30(3), 678–705. doi:10.1093/icc/dtaa049. Category definitions: Table 7.
  5. Irish patent register. Complete register of Irish patents, 1708–1852, provided by Stephen Billington, with patentees, domiciles and descriptions. The annual chart and topic classification are derived from this sheet.
  6. Comparative patenting series. Annual patentees per 1,000 persons, 1800–1899. For the underlying British patent dataset, see Berkes, Chen and Tranchero, 300 years of British patents.
  7. Patent Law Amendment Act 1852. 15 & 16 Vict. c. 83. Original Act.
  8. Patents, Designs, and Trade Marks Act 1883. 46 & 47 Vict. c. 57. Original Act.

The comparative CSV preserves blank observations as missing values. The classification download retains the two records with unrecorded domicile and the unresolved year discrepancy. The method file documents the counting rules and classification decisions.
